what: Fortune Brands Innovations makes products for homes. Its brands cover plumbing — Moen taps and showers — along with entry doors, door and window hardware, security products and decking. Most of it is sold through home improvement retailers and building suppliers.
customers: Homeowners renovating, builders constructing new houses, and plumbers and contractors specifying products, reached mainly through large home improvement chains and wholesale distributors.
money: Moen and related plumbing brands: taps, showers, waste disposal and connected water products.
Therma-Tru entry doors, Larson storm doors, Fiberon decking and Master Lock security products.
Door and window hardware and related building products.
moat: Moen is one of the few genuinely strong consumer brands in plumbing, which matters because a homeowner replacing a tap recognises very few names and a plumber recommends what they trust. Shelf space at the large home improvement retailers is also a real barrier: those chains carry two or three brands per category and changing supplier is a decision made rarely.
risks: Revenue has declined every year, from $4.8B in 2021 to $4.5B in 2025, as home renovation activity slowed.
Reported net income of $128.0M against $554.6M of free cash flow indicates writedowns, so the price/earnings ratio of 44.2 is not comparable to a normal year.
Debt of $2.8B against $264.0M of cash is heavy against a declining revenue line.
Home improvement spending depends on housing turnover and mortgage rates, both of which have worked against the business.
Seventeen analysts average a $49.29 target, only 4% above the current price.
opportunities: Free cash flow of $554.6M against a $5.6B market value is a 10% yield, and the shares trade at about 10.1 times free cash flow.
Moen is a genuinely valuable brand in a category where consumers recognise almost no names.
Shelf space at the large home improvement chains is a durable position that is rarely reallocated.
Housing stock in the United States is old and under-supplied, which supports renovation demand over time.
Connected water products — leak detection and shut-off — add a technology layer that justifies higher prices.
watch: Organic revenue growth and gross margin, separated from acquisitions and writedowns. The reported earnings are distorted; the underlying volume and the margin on it are what matter.
view: Fortune Brands is a collection of decent home products brands waiting for a housing cycle to turn, and the waiting has been expensive. Revenue has declined every year since 2021 — $4.8 billion to $4.5 billion — because home renovation activity depends on housing turnover, and housing turnover collapsed when mortgage rates rose. Homeowners sitting on cheap mortgages do not move, and people who do not move do not renovate kitchens.

The brands themselves are worth something real. Moen is one of very few names a homeowner recognises in plumbing, which is a category where consumers have almost no brand knowledge and therefore rely heavily on the one name they have heard of or on what their plumber recommends. Shelf space at the large home improvement chains is a quieter advantage: those retailers carry two or three brands per category and reallocate that space rarely, so an incumbent position is worth defending and very hard to attack.

The reported earnings are not usable. Net income of $128 million against $554 million of free cash flow means writedowns are doing the work, and the 44 times price/earnings ratio is an artefact. The honest multiple is about 10 times free cash flow for a 10% cash yield, which is a reasonable price for building products brands with no growth. Against that, $2.8 billion of debt on a declining revenue line is the thing that would turn a slow cycle into a problem.

What makes the eventual recovery likely rather than hopeful is the condition of the American housing stock: it is old, there is not enough of it, and the deferred renovation backlog grows every year that turnover stays frozen. That spending happens eventually. The difficulty is that seventeen analysts see 4% of upside, which says the market has already decided this is fairly valued for the wait. I would own this for the cash yield and the brands, judged on organic revenue and gross margin, and I would not expect the timing to be kind.
bull: Housing turnover recovers and releases a deferred renovation backlog, Moen’s brand and shelf position capture it, and a 10% free cash flow yield pays for the wait.
bear: Mortgage rates keep housing frozen for years, revenue declines further, and $2.8 billion of debt against a shrinking business forces harder choices.
